216  THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE

CHARACTER OF THE PROJECT

    The material of which the walls are built is a native stone, found a few miles north of town. It is described by competent builders as being a very superior building stone because of its flint-like nature. A building properly constructed as it is of this firm texture stone and reinforced concrete, will last indefinitely. There has been no finer building, based on the over-all cost, constructed in recent years in the Dallas areas by the Works Progress Administration.

    The revised project includes much ground work in the way of leveling and landscaping, with football and baseball fields, tennis courts, etc.

    The building as it stands today is practically completed, and the project as a whole is expected to be completed within two weeks. I desire in a formal way to call briefly to your attention to a few items: (1) Number one quality of native flooring has been used in this building, whereas a number two or three quality is usually used; (2) Bolts instead of nails are used throughout in the construction of the roof and bleachers, making it far more substantial; (3) All mill work is of prime quality and design; and (4) The seating arrangement is permanent bleachers with seating capacity of 600. In fact, no important detail has been overlooked. It has been an object of our earnestness in the performance of this work.


AS A MEMORIAL

    At the time of the laying of the cornerstone on September 19, 1937, the Board of Trustees of the Savoy Independent School District, and by formal resolution, named the building aside and dedicated of this building. This completed as a memorial to the late Warren Halsell, founder of the original school. Over the main entrance there has been placed a stone nameplate bearing the words Halsell Memorial. In addition to this, over the entrance there has been placed another stone bearing a dedicatory inscription.


AN UNUSUAL PROJECT

    These features therefore characterize an unusual project. The fact that a reunion of ex-students of the old school is being held at time of the dedication is also unusual in the history of WPA. This was deemed of sufficient of the National News Service as noteworthy, and both news gathering associations in the field have not out over their wires to all sections of the United States.
